<reason>Both sides were sharp, but PRO kept the debate anchored to the motion as written ("four-day weeks as adopted, not as imagined") while CON's core move—"a policy with an avoidable failure mode cannot harm more than it helps"—quietly swaps the aggregate comparison for "does a harmless version exist." PRO's "same dial" argument (the districts that cut time are the ones that save the most, so CON cannot pocket the savings of time-cutters while disowning their reading scores) was the most decisive analytical point, and CON's reply only asserted a "middle stop" without disputing the correlation. PRO also correctly caught CON stretching the "small or near zero" concession from time-holders to all adopters. CON scored real hits—the eight-hour-day inflation, PRO's vagueness about what share of districts actually hold hours, and the unaddressed "churn depresses achievement" mechanism—and honestly declined to invent a precise share. But CON's route to victory depended on misattributing PRO's concession, and PRO carried its burden more cleanly. PRO's two clipped turns and reliance on an asserted "most districts cut time" keep this competitive rather than solid.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [A4.5]/[A5.1] "same dial" charge—that CON counts every district as a time-holder for benefits and a time-cutter for harms, and that savings peak exactly where learning loss lives—which CON never squarely disputed, answering only with an asserted middle stop in [B5.3].</best_rebuttal>
